name: Stinging nettle
caution: A sting is not an identification test. Do not eat raw stinging foliage.

name: Dandelion
caution: Sap may irritate skin. Food use does not establish the safety or effectiveness of concentrated products.

name: Common yarrow
caution: Can cause contact dermatitis. Do not identify by a flat white flower cluster alone.

name: Black elder
caution: Raw or unripe berries and leaves or stems contain cyanide-producing substances. Do not use them.

name: American wild mint
caution: Pennyroyal is also a mint and is harmful if eaten. Hybrids complicate identification.

name: Red clover
caution: Check with a clinician before herbal use, especially during pregnancy, breastfeeding or when taking medicines.

name: Greater plantain
caution: Road margins, sprayed paths and pet-used lawns are poor gathering sites.

name: Mugwort
caution: NCCIH advises against use during pregnancy. Evidence for claimed health effects is limited.

name: Dog rose
caution: Wild roses are difficult to separate. Avoid ornamental shrubs with an unknown spray history.

name: Lemon balm
caution: Scent alone does not identify a plant. Confirm leaf arrangement and flowers as well.

name: German chamomile
caution: Allergic reactions can be severe, especially with daisy-family allergies. Medicine interactions are possible.

name: Calendula
caution: The common name marigold also refers to Tagetes. Ornamental nursery plants may have unsuitable pesticide treatments.

name: Wild garlic
caution: Lily of the valley and autumn crocus can grow among ramsons. Garlic scent transferred to hands can mislead.

name: Common purslane
caution: Contains oxalates; avoid large intakes. Rule out spurges before any food use.

name: Common chickweed
caution: Avoid mixing several groundcover species. Flowerless fragments are especially easy to confuse.

name: Yellow wood sorrel
caution: Large amounts can be harmful because of oxalates. Sour taste is never an identification test.

name: Sheep sorrel
caution: Contains substantial oxalic acid. Do not taste uncertain arrow-shaped leaves.

name: Garlic mustard
caution: A garlic smell alone cannot identify it. Do not spread mature seed during collection.

name: Cleavers
caution: Other bedstraws differ chemically. Do not infer edibility from a sticky stem.

name: Fennel
caution: Carrot-family mistakes can be fatal. Do not gather an unknown umbellifer by smell.

name: Watercress
caution: Wild watercress can carry liver flukes and contaminants. Clear water and rinsing do not establish safety.

name: Selfheal
caution: The common name heal-all is historical language, not evidence of medical effectiveness.

name: Common blue violet
caution: Do not identify a plant from a heart-shaped leaf alone. Ornamental African violets are unrelated.

name: Gotu kola
caution: Wild wet-ground plants can be contaminated. Food use is not evidence for concentrated supplements or treatment claims.

name: Lemongrass
caution: Other Cymbopogon species are grown for fragrance or oils. A lemon scent does not make them interchangeable.

name: Roselle
caution: Do not substitute ornamental hibiscus or identify by a red flower alone.

name: Moringa
caution: This entry covers food parts only. Do not infer that roots, bark, extracts or water-treatment claims are safe.

name: Culantro
caution: Leaf edges and flowering bracts can be sharp. It is not the same species as coriander.

name: Epazote
caution: Seeds in quantity and concentrated preparations can be dangerous. This guide supplies no home remedy or dose.

name: Lemon verbena
caution: Several plants are called verbena or yerba luisa. Do not substitute on the common name alone.

name: Perilla
caution: Color and aroma alone do not identify perilla. Keep it out of livestock grazing areas.

name: Warrigal greens
caution: Contains oxalic acid; do not present it as a raw salad green or unrestricted spinach substitute.

name: Lemon myrtle
caution: Other aromatic rainforest trees can resemble it. Confirm a named plant before use.

name: Kapokbos
caution: The name wild rosemary covers unrelated plants. Do not substitute it for culinary rosemary or ingest oils.

name: Rooibos
caution: Do not identify or harvest an unfamiliar fynbos shrub by needlelike leaves alone.

name: Round-leaf buchu
caution: Related buchus differ chemically. A traditional name does not identify a species or establish safety.

name: Poison hemlock
caution: All parts are highly poisonous. Small amounts can be fatal; obtain urgent poison-service advice after exposure.

name: Spotted water hemlock
caution: All parts are toxic and ingestion can be fatal. Seek urgent poison-service advice.

name: Lily of the valley
caution: Can cause serious poisoning including heart-rhythm disturbances. Seek prompt poison-service advice after ingestion.

name: Autumn crocus
caution: Colchicine poisoning can be fatal and symptoms may be delayed. Do not wait for illness before seeking help.

name: Foxglove
caution: Cardiac glycosides can cause serious, potentially fatal poisoning. Seek urgent advice after ingestion.

name: Pennyroyal
caution: The RHS explicitly identifies pennyroyal as non-edible and harmful if eaten.

name: Spotted spurge
caution: Sap can injure skin and eyes; ingestion irritates the mouth and digestive tract.

name: Common comfrey
caution: Ingestion can damage the liver. A history of medicinal use does not establish safety.

name: Wild strawberry
caution: Mock strawberry has yellow flowers and bland fruit; confirm white flowers.

name: Red raspberry
caution: Raspberry-leaf tea is widely promoted in pregnancy; evidence is limited, so ask a clinician.

name: Bilberry
caution: Several toxic berries grow in the same heath; check each plant.

name: Common hawthorn
caution: Hawthorn preparations can interact with heart medicines. Seeds contain cyanogenic compounds; strain them out.

name: Small-leaved lime
caution: Use modest amounts. Street trees collect traffic pollution, so gather from parks and woods away from roads.

name: Meadowsweet
caution: Contains salicylates. Avoid if allergic to aspirin, if taking blood thinners, or when advised against aspirin, including for children.

name: Lamb's quarters
caution: High in oxalate and can accumulate nitrate on fertilized soil. Avoid sprayed fields.

name: Miner's lettuce
caution: Contains some oxalate; eat in normal salad amounts.

name: Ramps
caution: Deadly false hellebore and lily of the valley grow in the same woods. Crush every leaf to check for onion smell.

name: Three-cornered leek
caution: Smell every plant. Snowdrops and snowflakes have similar white bells but no onion smell and are toxic.

name: Greater burdock
caution: Young rosettes can resemble foxglove and deadly nightshade leaves. Confirm burrs from last year nearby.

name: Chicory
caution: Roadside plants accumulate pollutants; gather away from traffic.

name: Ground ivy
caution: Toxic to horses in quantity. Use in modest amounts; avoid in pregnancy.

name: Wild oregano
caution: Concentrated oregano oil is not the same as the herb; avoid essential oil internally.

name: Field horsetail
caution: Contains thiaminase and can deplete vitamin B1. Not for long-term use, children, pregnancy, or people with kidney disease. Marsh horsetail is more toxic.

name: St John's wort
caution: Interacts with many medicines, including contraceptives, antidepressants, blood thinners and transplant drugs. Can cause sun sensitivity.

name: Common mullein
caution: Leaf hairs irritate the throat unless filtered. Seeds are toxic and have been used as a fish poison.

name: Ribwort plantain
caution: Plantain pollen is a common allergen.

name: Sea buckthorn
caution: Very sour; the juice can be irritating raw in quantity.

name: Common juniper
caution: Avoid in pregnancy and kidney disease. Other junipers, such as savin, are toxic.

name: Sweet woodruff
caution: Contains coumarin; large amounts cause headaches and liver concerns. Avoid with blood thinners.

name: Common sorrel
caution: High in oxalate. Avoid large amounts with kidney stones or gout.

name: Curly dock
caution: High in oxalate; large amounts can harm the kidneys. Not for people with kidney stones.

name: Common hop
caution: Hops can cause drowsiness. Hop cones are toxic to dogs.

name: Fireweed
caution: Large amounts can be laxative.

name: Wild bergamot
caution: Strong; use sparingly. Avoid in pregnancy.

name: Water mint
caution: Wash well; wild water can carry liver fluke and other parasites. Avoid pennyroyal confusion.

name: Prickly pear
caution: Glochids lodge in skin and are hard to remove. Handle with tongs and thick gloves.

name: Staghorn sumac
caution: Poison sumac has white, drooping berries and grows in swamps; never use white-berried sumacs. People with cashew or mango allergy may react.

name: Pawpaw
caution: Seeds and skin contain toxic compounds. Some people react with digestive upset or skin rash.

name: Saskatoon serviceberry
caution: Seeds contain small amounts of cyanogenic compounds; do not crush large quantities.

name: Chokecherry
caution: Pits, leaves and bark contain cyanogenic compounds. Never crush pits or brew leaves.

name: Common hazel
caution: Tree nut allergy is common and can be severe.

name: Glasswort
caution: Salt marshes can be polluted; harvest from clean coasts and follow local rules.

name: Wild carrot
caution: Deadly poison hemlock and water hemlock are close lookalikes. Hairy stems and carrot smell help but do not replace an expert check.

name: Cow parsley
caution: Poison hemlock and fool's parsley grow in the same hedges. Many experts recommend avoiding this plant entirely.

name: Shepherd's purse
caution: Avoid in pregnancy in medicinal amounts.

name: Borage
caution: Contains pyrrolizidine alkaloids that can harm the liver. Avoid regular use of leaves, and avoid in pregnancy.

name: Tamarind
caution: Pulp is mildly laxative in large amounts.

name: African baobab
caution: Respect community and customary ownership of trees.

name: African wormwood
caution: Contains thujone; large amounts are toxic to the nervous system. Avoid in pregnancy.

name: Spekboom
caution: Many succulents are toxic, including jade plant; confirm the species.

name: Holy basil
caution: Medicinal-strength use may affect blood sugar and blood clotting; ask a clinician.

name: Butterfly pea
caution: Seeds and roots are strongly laxative; use flowers only.

name: Water spinach
caution: Wild plants from polluted water can carry parasites and heavy metals; cook well. It is a regulated invasive in some countries.

name: Japanese knotweed
caution: Often sprayed with herbicide; ask the landowner. High in oxalate. Never move plant fragments, which regrow.

name: Yerba mate
caution: Contains caffeine. Very hot mate drunk regularly is linked to esophageal cancer; let it cool.

name: Maqui
caution: Confirm the plant; several shrubs with dark berries grow in the same forests.

name: Calafate
caution: Roots and bark contain berberine and are not for casual use.

name: Huacatay
caution: Use as a seasoning in small amounts; the oil can irritate skin.

name: Kawakawa
caution: Traditional practice selects insect-chewed leaves; follow guidance from Māori knowledge holders.

name: Mānuka
caution: Tea tree oil from Melaleuca is a different plant and is toxic if swallowed.

name: Sour fig
caution: Leaf juice is used on skin in traditional practice; confirm the species.

name: Purple passionflower
caution: Can cause drowsiness; avoid with sedatives and in pregnancy.

name: Valerian
caution: Can cause drowsiness and interact with sedatives. Not for use with alcohol or before driving.

name: Common mallow
caution: Can accumulate nitrate in fertilized soils.

name: Deadly nightshade
caution: All parts contain tropane alkaloids. A few berries can seriously poison a child. Seek urgent poison-service advice after any exposure.

name: Giant hogweed
caution: Sap on skin plus sunlight causes severe burns and long-lasting scars. Wash skin immediately, cover it from sun, and seek medical advice. Keep children and pets away.

name: Jimsonweed
caution: Tropane alkaloids cause delirium, fever, rapid heart rate and death. Seeds contaminate grain and vegetable crops. Seek urgent help after exposure.

name: American pokeweed
caution: Roots, mature stems, leaves and berries are poisonous. Traditional poke sallet uses specific preparation that does not make casual use safe.

name: Castor bean
caution: Seeds contain ricin; chewing even a few can be fatal. Keep seeds away from children and pets.

name: Oleander
caution: Contains cardiac glycosides. Leaves, flowers, sap and smoke from burning are dangerous. Never use stems as skewers.

name: Monkshood
caution: Contains aconitine, which can be absorbed through skin and causes fatal heart rhythm problems. Wear gloves in gardens and seek urgent care after exposure.

name: Meadow death camas
caution: All parts contain steroidal alkaloids. Bulbs have been confused with edible camas and wild onions, with fatal results.

name: Green false hellebore
caution: Highly toxic alkaloids cause vomiting, slowed heart rate and low blood pressure. Spring shoots have been mistaken for ramps and other greens.

name: Hemlock water dropwort
caution: Contains oenanthotoxin, which causes seizures and death. Roots have been mistaken for wild parsnip or carrot, and leaves for celery.

name: Lords-and-ladies
caution: Contains calcium oxalate crystals that burn the mouth and throat. Leaves grow among wild garlic and have been gathered by mistake.

name: European yew
caution: Contains taxine alkaloids that stop the heart. The red aril flesh is not toxic, but the seed inside is. Never eat any part.

name: Lantana
caution: Unripe berries and leaves are toxic to people and livestock and can cause liver damage and sun sensitivity in animals.
